Golam Rabbani with Mashuque Hosain Ahmed ----- For the Petitioner.
Santi Ranjan Karmaker ----- For Opposite Party.
parties:
Mohamaya Dutta ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Radha Ballav Sarkar ----- Opp. -Party
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J:- This Rule obtained u/s. 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and order dated 20-8-82 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. 4th Court. Dhaka in Misc. Case No. 34/77 dismissing the petitioner's application for permission to sue as a pauper, 

 2. The petitioner Mahamaya Dutta is a permanent resident of Calcutta. Her duly constituted Attorney Pijushkanti Chakraverty is a resident of Dhaka. Through the said attorney she filed Misc. Case No. 34/77 in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for permission to sue as a pauper a Title Suit for declaration of her title to the suit property at 7,Shankhari Bazar Road, Dhaka and recovery of possession of the ground and first floor against the Opposite party Radha Ballav Sarkar. She stated in her application that she is not possessed of sufficient means to enable her to pay the Court fees. 

 3. The Opposite party contested the case by filing a written objection. The petitioner did not appear in person, but her said attorney deposed as P. W. 1 and the Opposite party deposed as O.P.W. 2. By the impugned judgment and order the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the petitioner's application for permission to sue as a pauper. 

 5. We are frankly unable to accept the contention of Mr. Golam Rabbani. The petitioner did not annex in the application for permission to sue as a pauper the required particulars, namely, a schedule of any moveable or Immoveable property belonging to the petitioner, with the estimated value thereof Such particulars are required to be annexed to every application for permission to sue as a pauper. Failure to do the same will render the application an invalid one and because of this defect a petition to sue in forma pauperis should have been thrown out. We are supported in our view by a decision of a single judge of the then High Court of East Pakistan in the Case of The Sailakupa Co-Operative Multipurpose Society Ltd. Vs. Jahangir, 6 P.L.R. (Dhaka) 841. The fact that the petitioner as life interest in two urban properties at Dhaka came to be established not because of any disclosure made by the petitioner herself but because of a challenge thrown by the Opposite party and finally by an adjudication by the Court itself. In an application for leave to sue in forma pauperis, the utmost bona fide is required of the petitioner in the matter of the disclosure of his or her assets and any intentional departure from good faith whatever the motive might be must attract the consequence of a dismissal of the petition, because under Order 33, rule 2 read with Order 33 rule 5(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure, it is the bounden duty of the petitioner to make a full and accurate verified statement about his or her properties. The fact that even if the suppressed assets were disclosed, it would not affect the question of pauperism is not relevant. That is the view taken in two cases, namely. Kuppuswami Naidu Vs. Vardappa Naidu, A.I.R. 1943 Mad 11 and Chellamal Vs. Muthulakshmi Ammal, A.I.R. 1945 Mad 295. 

 6. It is because the petitioner herself did not make any disclosure about her properties in Dhaka that the Court was not under any obligation to assess for the purpose of payment of Court fees whether the interests fetched sufficient amount for such payment. If it was the case of the petitioner that she had life interests at Dhaka properties but the same were not possessed by her and they did not yield any income to her and if it was the case of the opposite party that this properties yielded income, then perhaps it was the duty of the Court to come to a finding along the lines urged by Mr. Rabbani. But when the facts are that the petitioner is emphatic about the fact that she has no properties in Bangladesh and the finding is that she has at least two life interests at Dhaka, such exercise as urged by Mr. Rabbani is not called for. 

 7. The submission that the life interest are not realisable assets is also misconceived because the word 'means' in Order 33 rule 1 is intended to cover and includes all forms of assets which can be converted into cash and it does not mean not having sufficient hard cash for the purpose (Jainutunnessa Vs. Idrakunnessa, A.I.R. 1941 Pat 638). As regards the assets in Calcutta and the moveable property of 27 tolas of gold the learned Subordinate Judge has not given any clear finding as to whether the petitioner owns and possesses the same. We find from the evidence on record however the agent of the petitioner has in a similar vein professed his ignorance about these properties as well and applying the well-known principles of denial we can tab it to be admitted that the petitioner is also possessed of the properties. Mr. Golam Rabbani submits that an asset in Calcutta will not be a consideration for determination as to whether the petitioner has sufficient means to pay Court fee in Bangladesh. We do not find any reason to hold that the word 'means' in order 33 rule 1 C.P.C. excludes foreign assets and properties and includes assets and properties only in Bangladesh. To hold so will be to allow rich and affluent foreigners holding no property in Bangladesh to merrily sue in forma pauperis in the Courts of Bangladesh. It will be and affront to commonsense if we were to hold that 'means' excludes foreign property and assets.
